records.question: Hello! In PEID, what surrounds the model in an AI assistant?

replies.content:
In an AI assistant, the model is wrapped in three other things [PEID-2.1]:

- **A system prompt and control loop** — written by whoever built the app [PEID-2.1].
- **Tools** — functions the app offers, described to the model in plain text; the model only writes a request, the app runs it and pastes the result back [PEID-2.1].
- **Memory** — the conversation re-sent each turn, plus anything the app stores [PEID-2.1].

Each turn the app assembles one token sequence, the model predicts, and if the output is a tool call the app runs it and loops; otherwise it shows the answer and stops. The model itself is stateless [PEID-2.1]. More broadly, the building block is a model with retrieval, tools and memory, and everything else is composition [PEID-4.2].

records.question: For PEID, explain how an assistant's model and tools interact.

replies.content:
An assistant is not just the model: it is the model wrapped in three other things — a **system prompt and control loop** written by whoever built the app, **tools** (functions the app offers, described to the model in plain text), and **memory** (the conversation re-sent each turn plus anything the app stores) [PEID-2.1].

How they interact on each turn: the app assembles one token sequence, the model predicts, and **if the output is a tool call the app runs it and loops**; otherwise it shows the answer and stops. The model itself only writes the request — the app executes it and pastes the result back — and the model is stateless [PEID-2.1].

Two consequences worth noting:
- Everything (system prompt, tool definitions, retrieved documents, history, user message) is concatenated into one flat token sequence with no fields, only position [PEID-2.2]; tool definitions are a standing cost paid on every call, so keep tool sets small enough that a colleague could tell the tools apart from their descriptions [PEID-3.4].
- When the answer is not in the model at all, thinking cannot produce it: ReAct interleaves Thought → Action (a tool call) → Observation (the result), repeated until the model decides it can answer — and that loop is the agent [PEID-2.9].

records.question: Can you explain that more simply?

history.content: Could you describe what context contributes to a prompt?
Context provides the background needed for the task [PEID-2.3].

replies.content:
Simply put: context is the input you give the model to work on — the material it should base its answer on, clearly separated from your instruction [PEID-2.3]. It is one of the six parts of a good prompt, alongside role, task, examples, constraints and the output contract [PEID-2.3].

Why it matters: the model predicts text rather than looking facts up, so if a fact is not in the context it will still produce an answer — which is how it invents specifics [PEID-1.9]. No wording fixes a missing fact; putting the relevant material in the window does [PEID-3.1].

records.question: Why does a digital transformation programme need changes to staff responsibilities as well as new software?

replies.content:
A digital transformation programme is not only a technology change, so the people side has to move with the software:

- Transformation means change and alignment across technology infrastructure, processes, the business model, products and services, work procedures **and people** — and "digital transformation is not only about technology" [DTGS-1.1].
- In Vial's process model, changes in value-creation paths are affected by **structural changes** — organisational structure, culture, leadership, and **employee roles and skills** — and held back by organisational barriers such as inertia and resistance [DTGS-1.2].
- The "change iceberg" explains why tooling alone fails: above the waterline sit technology, tools, licences, architecture and the demo; below sit incentives, ownership, skills, trust, status and fear of redundancy [DTGS-3.3].
- Resistance often comes from exactly these human factors: parochial self-interest, misunderstanding and lack of trust, different assessments, and low tolerance for change (fear of not being able to develop the new skills required) [DTGS-1.4]. Hence change management — defining the need for change, involving everyone, leading the change — and competence and training management are part of a holistic transformation methodology [DTGS-1.7].
- GenAI specifically requires reshaped and redesigned processes, organisational change, and employee upskilling and reskilling [DTGS-1.11]; and in the canvas, key activities shift so that review, exceptions and escalation become the real work — raising the question "have we redesigned the workflow, or accelerated the old one?" [DTGS-3.11].
- Leadership choice reflects the same point: an insider is favoured over a digital expert because transformation is about changing the organisation and its people [DTGS-1.8].

records.question: Why does a digital transformation programme need changes to staff responsibilities as well as new software?

replies.content:
A digital transformation programme is not only a technology effort: "digital" and "transformation" together mean changing technology infrastructure, processes, the business model, products and services, work procedures **and people**, aligned with business strategy to create value [DTGS-1.1]. Vial's sequence makes the same point structurally — changes in value-creation paths are affected by structural changes such as organisational structure, culture, leadership, and **employee roles and skills**, and are held back by organisational barriers like inertia and resistance [DTGS-1.2].

So new software alone leaves the human side of the change unaddressed:

- **Resistance is often about roles and skills, not tools.** People resist from parochial self-interest (what they personally lose), misunderstanding and lack of trust, different assessments, and low tolerance for change — including fear of not being able to develop the new skills required [DTGS-1.4]. Facilitation and support is the approach aimed specifically at such adjustment problems [DTGS-1.5].
- **Change management is a named discipline in the methodology**, alongside technology management: define the need for change, involve everyone, lead the change, plus competence and training management [DTGS-1.7]. ADKAR likewise runs through Awareness, Desire, Knowledge, Ability and Reinforcement for each individual [DTGS-1.7].
- **The "change iceberg"** explains why programmes fail: above the waterline sit technology, tools, licences, architecture and the demo; below sit incentives, ownership, skills, trust, status and fear of redundancy — and roughly 30% of transformation projects fail outright, suggesting the binding constraint was never the technology [DTGS-3.3].
- **Leadership should come from someone who can change the organisation and its people**, which requires credibility and knowledge of the business more than technical expertise [DTGS-1.8].
- **GenAI specifically requires reshaped processes, organisational change, and upskilling/reskilling of employees** [DTGS-1.11]; value leaks through weak governance (no owner, no escalation path) and misaligned incentives [DTGS-3.2], and workflow/accountability is one of the layers you must own yourself [DTGS-3.6].

- In Vial's sequence, changes in value-creation paths are affected by **structural changes** — organisational structure, culture, leadership, and **employee roles and skills** — and held back by organisational barriers such as inertia and resistance [DTGS-1.2].
- Resistance often stems from people's fear that they cannot develop the new skills and behaviour required, or from a sense of personal loss, so the change strategy has to address roles and capabilities, not just systems [DTGS-1.4]. The ADKAR model likewise treats individual Knowledge, Ability and Reinforcement as phases of a change [DTGS-1.7].
- The "change iceberg" explains why programmes fail: above the waterline sit technology, tools, licences and the demo; below sit incentives, ownership, skills, trust, status and fear of redundancy — and the binding constraint was never the technology [DTGS-3.3].
- GenAI specifically requires processes to be reshaped and redesigned, with employees upskilled and reskilled [DTGS-1.11]; and value leaks where workflows are not redesigned, e.g. where review, exceptions and escalation become the real work [DTGS-3.2] [DTGS-3.11].
